preamble.whatYouWillLearn: You will use circuit symbols to read and describe circuit diagrams. You will compare how bright lamps are in series and parallel circuits. You will also find out why a circuit might not work and how to test materials fairly.
preamble.whyItMatters: Torches, doorbells, phone chargers and the lights in your home all depend on circuits. Knowing how circuits work helps you build them, find simple faults and stay safe around electricity.
realWorld: Old strings of festive fairy lights: when one bulb breaks, the whole string can go dark because the bulbs are in series
The lights in your home are wired in parallel, so you can switch on the kitchen light without the bedroom light
A torch uses two or more cells in series to make its bulb bright
A doorbell is a simple circuit: the button is a switch and the bell is a buzzer
Phone charger cables have copper inside (a conductor) and plastic outside (an insulator) to keep you safe

subtopics.title: Circuit symbols and complete circuits
subtopics.summary: Recognise the symbols for a cell, battery, lamp, buzzer, switch, wire and junction, and know that a lamp lights only in a complete loop.

subtopics.title: Series circuits
subtopics.summary: In a series circuit everything is in one loop: more lamps make each lamp dimmer, more cells make them brighter, and one break stops everything.

subtopics.title: Parallel circuits
subtopics.summary: In a parallel circuit each lamp has its own branch, so lamps stay bright and keep working if another branch is broken.

subtopics.title: Conductors, insulators and fixing circuits
subtopics.summary: Metals conduct electricity and plastics, rubber and wood insulate. Use this, and fair tests, to find out why a circuit does not work.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. What is the component labelled X?

diagram.alt: A circuit diagram with three components joined in one loop. One of them is labelled X.

questions.solution: Component X is drawn as a circle with a cross inside. That is the symbol for a lamp. You can remember it because the cross looks a little like the glowing wire inside a bulb. The other two symbols in the loop are a cell and a closed switch.

misconceptions.0: The cell is a different symbol in this circuit: a long thin line next to a short thick line. X is a circle with a cross, which is a lamp.
misconceptions.1: A buzzer has its own symbol, and there is no buzzer in this circuit. The circle with a cross is the lamp.
misconceptions.3: The switch in this circuit is the short line lying flat across a gap. It has no circle. X is a circle with a cross, so it is a lamp.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. Which component is the cell?

diagram.alt: A circuit diagram with four components joined in one loop, labelled A, B, C and D.

questions.solution: A cell is drawn as two lines side by side: a long thin line and a short thick line. That is component A. The long line is the positive (+) side. B is a lamp, C is an open switch and D is a buzzer.

misconceptions.1: B is a circle with a cross inside. That is the lamp symbol.
misconceptions.2: C is a line with a gap, where a short line is lifted up. That is an open switch, which makes a gap so electricity cannot flow.
misconceptions.3: D is the buzzer symbol. A buzzer makes a sound; it does not push electricity. A cell is drawn as a long thin line next to a short thick line.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. Match each labelled symbol to the component it shows.

diagram.alt: A circuit diagram with five symbols joined in one loop, labelled A, B, C, D and E.

questions.solution: A is a circle with a cross: a lamp. B is a long thin line next to a short thick line: a cell. C has a gap with a lifted line: an open switch. D is a circle with the letter M inside: a motor. E is the buzzer symbol. A closed switch would have its line lying flat across the gap, and a junction is a large dot where wires join; neither of these is in this circuit.

misconceptions.common: Mixing up the open and the closed switch. If the line is lifted, there is a gap, so the switch is OPEN. Also look carefully at the circles: a cross inside means a lamp, and the letter M inside means a motor.

questions.prompt: True or false: When a switch in a simple circuit is open, electricity flows and the lamp lights.
questions.solution: False. An open switch leaves a gap in the circuit, so there is no complete loop. Electricity cannot flow and the lamp stays off. Closing the switch joins the gap and the lamp lights.

misconceptions.common: In everyday life we say 'open the tap' to make water flow, so some people think an 'open' switch lets electricity flow. In circuits it is the other way round: open means a gap, so OFF.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. Switch P is open and switch Q is closed. How is the symbol for the CLOSED switch different from the symbol for the OPEN switch?

diagram.alt: A circuit diagram: a cell, a lamp and two switches, P and Q, joined in one loop. Switch P is open and switch Q is closed.

options: In a closed switch a cross is drawn over the switch to show it is off
In a closed switch the gap is drawn wider so that no electricity can pass
In a closed switch there is a long line next to a short line
In a closed switch the short line lies flat across the gap, joining both sides
questions.solution: Look at switch Q, the closed switch: its short line lies flat and touches both sides, so the gap is joined. In switch P, the open switch, the short line is lifted and there is a gap. (In this circuit the lamp is off, because switch P is open.)

misconceptions.0: A cross inside a circle is the lamp symbol. Switches never have a cross.
misconceptions.1: This mixes up the words. 'Closed' means the gap is closed (joined), so electricity CAN pass. Think of a drawbridge: when it comes down flat, the gap is closed and you can cross.
misconceptions.2: A long line next to a short line is the cell symbol, not a switch.

questions.prompt: What is the name for two or more cells joined together in a circuit?
questions.solution: Two or more cells joined together make a battery. In everyday life we call a single AA cell a 'battery', but in science one is a cell and two or more joined together make a battery.

misconceptions.common: Answering 'cells' or 'cell'. One cell on its own is a cell; joined cells make a battery.

questions.prompt: Look at circuits A to F. Every part works properly. In circuit E, a plastic ruler is clipped across the gap. Select ALL the circuits in which the lamp will light.
questions.solution: A lamp lights only when there is a complete loop of conductors from the cell, through the lamp and back. Circuits A, C (closed switch) and F (two cells joined as a battery) are complete loops, so their lamps light. Circuit B has a gap, circuit D has an open switch, and in circuit E the plastic ruler does not conduct.

misconceptions.1: Circuit B has a gap in the wire, so there is no complete loop. Electricity needs a path out of the cell, through the lamp and back again.
misconceptions.3: In circuit D the switch is open. An open switch makes a gap, so the loop is not complete.
misconceptions.4: In circuit E the gap is bridged only by a plastic ruler. Plastic is an electrical insulator, so it acts like a gap.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. What happens when the circuit is set up as shown?
options: The lamp lights but the buzzer is silent, because the lamp uses up the electricity first
The lamp is off and the buzzer is silent, because the switch is open
The lamp lights and the buzzer sounds
Only the buzzer sounds, because it is the component nearest to the switch
questions.solution: First name each symbol in the diagram: a cell, a lamp, a buzzer and an open switch. They are all in one loop (a series circuit). The switch is open, so there is a gap and no electricity can flow. Nothing works until the switch is closed, and then both the lamp and the buzzer work.

misconceptions.0: Electricity is not used up by the first component. In any case, the switch is open, so nothing works at all.
misconceptions.2: Look again at the switch symbol. The lifted line means the switch is open, so the loop is broken.
misconceptions.3: Being near the switch does not matter. In a single loop, an open switch stops the electricity everywhere.

questions.prompt: The circuit diagram shows a series circuit with one cell and one lamp. You add a second, identical lamp in series. What happens?
options: Both lamps are dimmer than the single lamp was
Both lamps are brighter than the single lamp was
The first lamp stays as bright as before and the second lamp is dim
Nothing changes; both lamps are as bright as the single lamp was
questions.solution: In a series circuit everything is in one loop. With a second lamp in the loop, the push from the one cell is shared by two lamps, so both lamps glow more dimly than the single lamp did, and they are equally bright.

misconceptions.1: More lamps do not mean more light from each lamp. The two lamps share the push from one cell, so each is dimmer.
misconceptions.2: Electricity is not used up by the first lamp. In a series circuit the lamps are the same brightness.
misconceptions.3: That would be true for lamps in parallel, not in series. In series the lamps share the cell, so each one is dimmer.

questions.prompt: Look at the series circuit with three lamps, A, B and C. True or false: If lamp B breaks, lamps A and C go out as well.
questions.solution: True. The diagram shows one single loop, so there is only one path. A broken lamp B makes a gap in that path, so the electricity stops everywhere and lamps A and C go out too.

misconceptions.common: Thinking the other lamps keep working. That happens in a parallel circuit, where each lamp has its own path.

questions.prompt: Look at the series circuit: one cell and two lamps. You add a second cell, facing the same way as the first. What happens to the lamps?
options: Both lamps become dimmer, because there are more components in the circuit
Only the lamp next to the new cell becomes brighter
Nothing changes, because a circuit only uses one cell at a time
questions.solution: Two cells in series give a bigger push than one cell. With the same two lamps, more electricity flows, so both lamps glow brighter.

misconceptions.0: Adding a LAMP makes lamps dimmer. Adding a CELL gives a bigger push, so the lamps get brighter.
misconceptions.1: In a series circuit the lamps are always equally bright. The extra push from the new cell reaches the whole loop.
misconceptions.3: Cells joined in series all push together, so the push is bigger.

questions.prompt: All cells and lamps are identical and every circuit is a series circuit. Put the circuits in order from the DIMMEST lamps to the BRIGHTEST lamps.
questions.solution: Think 'push from the cells' shared between the lamps. 1 cell shared by 3 lamps is the dimmest. 1 cell shared by 2 lamps is next. 1 cell with 1 lamp is brighter. 2 cells with only 1 lamp is the brightest.

misconceptions.common: Looking only at the number of cells or only at the number of lamps. You need both: more cells make lamps brighter, more lamps in series make each lamp dimmer.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. All three lamps are lit. One lamp is unscrewed and taken out. How many lamps are still lit? Give a whole number.
questions.solution: Taking out one lamp leaves a gap in the only path. In a series circuit a gap anywhere stops all the electricity, so 0 lamps stay lit.

misconceptions.common: Answering 2 by thinking the other lamps keep working. That only happens when lamps are in parallel.

questions.prompt: True or false: In a series circuit with two identical lamps, the lamp nearer the positive (+) end of the cell is brighter because it gets the electricity first.
questions.solution: False. Electricity flows all the way round the loop at the same time; it is not used up as it goes. Identical lamps in series are equally bright, wherever they are in the loop.

misconceptions.common: Thinking electricity is 'used up' as it travels, so the first lamp takes most of it. The current is the same in every part of a series circuit.

questions.prompt: Arjun investigates this question: 'How does the number of lamps in a series circuit affect how bright each lamp is?' He uses 1, 2, 3 and then 4 lamps. Which is the INDEPENDENT variable (the one he changes)?
questions.solution: The independent variable is the one thing you choose to change: here, the number of lamps. The dependent variable is what you measure (brightness). Everything else, such as the number of cells and the type of wire, stays the same.

misconceptions.0: Brightness is what he observes or measures. That is the dependent variable.
misconceptions.1: He keeps the number of cells the same. That is a control variable, so the test is fair.
misconceptions.2: He should keep the wires the same. That is a control variable.

questions.prompt: Wei Ming measures how bright a lamp is with a light sensor. He tests each number of cells three times. Results: 1 cell: 20, 21, 19. 2 cells: 40, 12, 41. 3 cells: 60, 59, 61. Which reading is the anomalous result (the one that does not fit the pattern)? Give the number.
questions.solution: The other two readings for 2 cells are 40 and 41, and the pattern goes up by about 20 for each extra cell. The reading 12 is far away from the rest, so it is anomalous. Wei Ming should check his circuit and repeat that reading.

misconceptions.common: Choosing 19 or 59 because they are a little lower. Small differences are normal; an anomalous result is one that is far away from the others.

questions.prompt: All cells and lamps are identical. Look at the series circuits A to D. Which circuit has lamps that glow with the SAME brightness as a circuit with 1 cell and 1 lamp?
questions.solution: Count the cells and the lamps in each circuit. With 1 cell and 1 lamp, each lamp gets the push of one cell. Circuit B has 2 cells and 2 lamps: the push of two cells is shared by two lamps, so each lamp again gets the push of one cell. The brightness is the same.

misconceptions.0: Circuit A has two lamps sharing the push from only one cell, so each lamp is dimmer.
misconceptions.2: Circuit C has two cells pushing one lamp, so its lamp is brighter than 1 cell with 1 lamp.
misconceptions.3: Circuit D has three cells shared by two lamps. That gives each lamp more push than one cell, so they are brighter.

questions.prompt: Mei Lin hangs an old string of fairy lights for Hari Raya. At the moment one tiny bulb breaks, ALL the other bulbs go out, even though they all work. What is the best explanation?
options: The broken bulb has used up all the electricity
The bulbs are joined in parallel, so one broken bulb stops them all
The bulbs are joined in series, so the broken bulb makes a gap in the only path
The bulbs are all on separate branches, so each one needs its own cell
questions.solution: A string where one broken bulb puts out all the others must have its bulbs in series: one single loop. The broken bulb breaks the loop, so no electricity flows through any bulb.

misconceptions.0: Bulbs do not use up the electricity flowing through them. The problem is the gap that the broken bulb makes.
misconceptions.1: This is the wrong way round. In parallel, the other bulbs would stay lit because each has its own path.
misconceptions.3: Separate branches would be a parallel circuit, and the other bulbs would still light from the same supply.

questions.prompt: Which sentence describes lamps joined in PARALLEL?
options: The lamps are joined one after another in a single loop
Each lamp is on its own separate branch connected to the cell
The lamps must be touching each other
The lamps are lined up in a straight row next to each other
questions.solution: In a parallel circuit the wires split into branches. Each lamp sits on its own branch, so each lamp has its own path back to the cell.

misconceptions.0: One single loop is a series circuit.
misconceptions.2: Lamps in a circuit are joined by wires; they do not need to touch.
misconceptions.3: 'Parallel' in maths means lines side by side, but in circuits it means separate branches (paths), not the way the lamps are lined up.

questions.prompt: True or false: In a parallel circuit, if the lamp on one branch breaks, the lamps on the other branches stay lit.
questions.solution: True. Each branch is its own path. A break in one branch does not affect the complete paths through the other branches.

misconceptions.common: Thinking all the lamps go out. That happens in a series circuit, which has only one path.

questions.prompt: What type of circuit has more than one path (branch) for the electricity to flow along?
questions.solution: A parallel circuit has two or more branches, so electricity has more than one path to follow.

misconceptions.common: Answering 'series'. A series circuit has only ONE path.

questions.prompt: The circuit diagram shows a cell with two identical lamps in parallel. Compared with ONE of these lamps connected on its own to the same cell, how bright is each lamp?
options: One lamp is bright and the other is dim
questions.solution: In a parallel circuit each lamp is on its own branch and gets the full push from the cell. So each lamp is about as bright as a single lamp on the same cell. (The cell does run down faster, because it is lighting two lamps.)

misconceptions.0: That is what happens in SERIES, where lamps share one path. In parallel, each lamp gets the full push of the cell.
misconceptions.1: The cell has not changed, so the push on each lamp is the same, not bigger.
misconceptions.2: The lamps are identical and each is on its own branch, so they are equally bright.

questions.prompt: Why are the lights in a home wired in parallel, not in series?
options: So each light can be switched on and off by itself, and the others keep working if one bulb blows
So that all the lights go off together to save electricity
Because parallel wiring uses fewer wires than series wiring
So that the lights are dimmer and use less electricity
questions.solution: With parallel wiring, every light is on its own branch with its own switch. You can turn on the kitchen light without the bedroom light, and a blown bulb does not put out the others.

misconceptions.1: That would happen in series wiring, and it would be very inconvenient: you could not light just one room.
misconceptions.2: Parallel wiring usually needs MORE wire, because each branch needs its own path. It is chosen for convenience and reliability.
misconceptions.3: In parallel each light gets the full push and stays bright. Lights in series would be the dim ones.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the true statements. Look at the circuit diagram: the identical lamps P, Q and R are each on their own parallel branch. Lamp Q breaks.
options: Lamps P and R both go out
Lamps P and R become much dimmer
questions.solution: Q's branch now has a gap, so Q is off. In the diagram, P and R are on separate branches that are still complete loops with the cell, so they stay lit and about as bright as before.

misconceptions.2: That would happen in series. Here P and R are on their own branches, which are still complete.
misconceptions.3: P and R still get the full push from the cell on their own branches, so they stay about as bright as before.

questions.prompt: Look at circuits A and B. Each has one cell and two lamps, and all the cells and lamps are identical. In which circuit are the lamps brighter?
options: All four lamps are equally bright
questions.solution: Circuit A is a series circuit: the two lamps share one path and one cell, so each is dim. Circuit B is a parallel circuit: each lamp has its own branch and gets the full push of the cell, so each is as bright as a single lamp. So the lamps in circuit B are brighter. (Both lamps in B light, because electricity flows through every complete branch at the same time.)

misconceptions.0: This is the wrong way round. In series (circuit A) the two lamps share the push of the cell, so they are dimmer.
misconceptions.2: Having the same parts is not enough. The way they are joined changes the brightness: lamps in parallel are brighter than lamps in series.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. The lamp and the buzzer both worked while the switch was closed. The switch has now been opened, as shown. What happens?
options: The lamp and the buzzer both stop
The lamp stays on and the buzzer stops
The lamp goes off and the buzzer keeps sounding
Nothing changes, because switches do not work in parallel circuits
questions.solution: The switch is on the lamp's branch only. Opening it makes a gap in that branch, so the lamp goes off. The buzzer's branch still makes a complete loop with the cell, so the buzzer keeps sounding.

misconceptions.0: That would be true in a series circuit. The switch is only on branch 1, so branch 2 is still a complete path.
misconceptions.1: A switch only controls the branch it is on. This switch is on the lamp's branch, not the buzzer's.
misconceptions.3: Switches work in any circuit. This one breaks the path through branch 1, so the lamp goes off.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. The switch is in the main wire next to the cell, before the circuit splits into two branches. True or false: Opening this switch turns off only one of the lamps.
questions.solution: False. In the diagram, all the electricity has to pass through the switch before the circuit splits. Opening the switch breaks the path for both branches, so BOTH lamps go off.

misconceptions.common: Thinking any switch in a parallel circuit controls only one lamp. It depends where the switch is: on a branch it controls that branch; in the main wire before the split it controls everything.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the materials that conduct electricity.
questions.solution: Metals are good electrical conductors: copper, aluminium and steel all let electricity pass. Plastic, rubber and dry wood are insulators.

misconceptions.1: Plastic is an insulator. That is why it is used to cover wires.
misconceptions.3: Rubber is an insulator.

questions.prompt: Why are the copper wires in a lamp cable covered in plastic?
options: Plastic is a good conductor, so it helps carry the electricity
Plastic makes the electricity flow faster
The plastic is only there to give the cable a nice colour
Plastic is an electrical insulator, so it stops electricity passing into anyone who touches the cable
questions.solution: Copper conducts electricity well, so it carries the electricity. Plastic is an insulator, so wrapping it round the copper keeps the electricity inside the wire and keeps people safe.

misconceptions.0: This is the wrong way round. The COPPER inside is the conductor; the plastic is an insulator.
misconceptions.1: The plastic does not carry the electricity at all. Its job is to keep it safely inside the wire.
misconceptions.2: Colours help us tell wires apart, but the main reason is safety: plastic is an insulator.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. The parts are joined in a complete loop with copper wires and the switch is closed, but the lamp does not light. Which of these could be the reason?
options: The thin wire (filament) inside the lamp is broken
The wires are made of copper
The wires are 30 cm long, so the electricity cannot reach the lamp
questions.solution: If the filament inside the bulb is broken, there is a gap inside the lamp itself, so the loop is not complete and the lamp cannot light. Other things to check would be a flat cell or a loose connection.

misconceptions.0: A closed switch joins the gap, so it lets electricity flow. It would be a problem if the switch were OPEN.
misconceptions.2: Copper is an excellent conductor. That is why it is used for wires.
misconceptions.3: Electricity flows easily through 30 cm of copper wire. Wires much longer than this are used in homes.

questions.prompt: True or false: Tap water can conduct electricity, so you should never touch a light switch or plug with wet hands.
questions.solution: True. Tap water has tiny amounts of dissolved substances that let electricity pass. Wet hands make it easier for electricity from the mains to pass through your body, which is very dangerous.

misconceptions.common: Thinking water is an insulator because it is not a metal. Tap water conducts electricity well enough to be dangerous with mains electricity.

questions.prompt: You want to test whether some objects conduct electricity. Which way of testing is the SAFEST?
options: Push each object into the holes of a wall socket and see if anything happens
Use a circuit with one cell, but hold the bare ends of the wires with wet hands
Use a circuit with one cell, a lamp and wires, and put each object in a gap in the circuit
Use the cable of a plugged-in lamp, after cutting it open, and touch the objects to the wires
questions.solution: Cells give a small, safe push. A simple tester circuit with a cell, a lamp and a gap is safe to use: if the lamp lights when an object closes the gap, the object is a conductor. Never experiment with mains electricity.

misconceptions.0: Mains electricity from a wall socket can kill. Never put anything into a socket.
misconceptions.1: Wet hands are a bad habit around electricity. Keep hands dry and hold wires by their plastic coating.
misconceptions.3: Cutting a mains cable is extremely dangerous. School tests should only use cells.

questions.prompt: Priya builds the circuit shown in the diagram, with a gap between two crocodile clips. She clips different objects into the gap. How can she tell that an object is an electrical conductor?
options: The lamp lights when the object is clipped into the gap
The object gets warm in her hand
The lamp goes out when the object is clipped into the gap
The crocodile clips stick to the object
questions.solution: In the diagram the gap breaks the circuit, so the lamp is off. A conductor fills the gap and completes the loop, so electricity flows and the lamp lights. An insulator leaves the lamp off.

misconceptions.1: Warmth is not how we test for electrical conductors here. The lamp is the sign that electricity is flowing.
misconceptions.2: With a gap, the lamp is already off. A conductor completes the loop, so the lamp turns ON.
misconceptions.3: This mixes up electrical conductors with magnetic materials. Sticking is about magnets, not electricity.

questions.prompt: Priya's results: steel spoon - lamp lit; plastic spoon - not lit; wooden spoon - not lit; aluminium foil - lit; glass marble - not lit. Which conclusion do her results support best?
options: The metal objects conducted electricity and the other objects did not
Heavy objects conduct electricity and light objects do not
questions.solution: Look for what the 'lit' objects have in common: the steel spoon and the aluminium foil are both metals. The plastic, wood and glass objects did not light the lamp. So the results support: metals conduct electricity; these non-metals do not.

misconceptions.0: Only the steel spoon lit the lamp. The plastic and wooden spoons did not, so the shape of the object does not matter: the material does.
misconceptions.2: The glass marble is shiny, but it did not light the lamp. Shininess is not the reason; being a metal is.
misconceptions.3: Aluminium foil is very light, but it lit the lamp. Mass is not what matters.

questions.prompt: Omar wants to find out whether the length of wire in a circuit affects how bright a lamp is. Which plan is a fair test?
options: Change the length of the wire and also add an extra cell for the longer wires
Use a different lamp for each length of wire, to make it more interesting
Test only one length of wire, but test it ten times
Change only the length of the wire, and keep the same cell, lamp and type of wire each time
questions.solution: In a fair test you change ONE thing (the independent variable: wire length), measure one thing (the dependent variable: brightness) and keep everything else the same (control variables: cell, lamp, type and thickness of wire).

misconceptions.0: This changes two things at once. If the brightness changes, he would not know which change caused it.
misconceptions.1: Different lamps could be brighter or dimmer on their own, so the test would not be fair.
misconceptions.2: Repeating is good, but with only one length he cannot see whether length makes a difference.

questions.prompt: Aisha builds a series circuit with two cells and one lamp. All the parts work and the wires are joined properly, but the lamp does not light. When she turns ONE of the cells round, the lamp lights brightly. Why did the lamp not light at first?
options: The two cells were facing opposite ways, so their pushes worked against each other and cancelled out
Two cells give too much electricity for one lamp
The lamp needed time to warm up before it could light
Turning the cell round made the wires start to conduct
questions.solution: Cells push electricity one way round the circuit, from the + side. If two cells face opposite ways, one pushes clockwise and the other anticlockwise, so they cancel out and the lamp stays off. Turned the same way, their pushes add up and the lamp lights brightly.

misconceptions.1: If that were true, the lamp would not light brightly after she turned the cell round, because there are still two cells.
misconceptions.2: Lamps light straight away in a complete circuit. The change came from turning the cell, not from waiting.
misconceptions.3: The copper wires always conduct. The wires did not change; the direction of one cell did.

questions.prompt: Look at circuits A to D. All the parts work. In which circuit will the lamp light?
questions.solution: A lamp lights only in a complete loop. Check each circuit for gaps and open switches. Circuit A has an open switch, circuit B has a gap, and circuit D has an open switch as well as a closed one. Only circuit C is a complete loop, so only its lamp lights.

misconceptions.0: In circuit A the switch is open. An open switch leaves a gap, so the loop is not complete.
misconceptions.1: Circuit B has a gap in the wire. Electricity cannot jump across the gap, so the lamp stays off.
misconceptions.3: Circuit D has one closed switch, but its other switch is open. One gap anywhere in the loop is enough to stop the electricity.

questions.prompt: You want a switch that turns lamp X off while lamp Y stays on. Look at circuits A to D. In which circuit will opening the switch do this?
questions.solution: A switch controls the lamps on the same path as itself. To turn off only lamp X, the switch must be on X's own branch of a parallel circuit, with Y on a separate branch. That is circuit D: opening its switch breaks X's branch, while Y's branch is still a complete loop with the cell.

misconceptions.0: Circuit A is a series circuit with one loop. Opening the switch breaks the only path, so both lamps go off.
misconceptions.1: In circuit B the switch is in the main wire before the circuit splits, so it turns off both lamps.
misconceptions.2: In circuit C the switch is on lamp Y's branch, so opening it turns off Y, not X.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. All three lamps are lit. Which switch should you open to turn off lamp C but leave lamps A and B lit?
options: Any one of the three switches
questions.solution: Find which path each switch is on. S1 is in the main wire before the circuit splits, so it controls all three lamps. S2 is on lamp A's branch. S3 is on lamp C's branch. Opening S3 makes a gap in C's branch only, so C goes off and A and B stay lit.

misconceptions.0: S1 is in the main wire before the circuit splits. Opening it turns off all three lamps.
misconceptions.1: S2 is on lamp A's branch. Opening it turns off lamp A, not lamp C.
misconceptions.3: Each switch controls a different part of the circuit, so only one of them does this job. Follow each switch to the lamps on the same path.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. Select ALL the lamps that are lit.
questions.solution: First check the main wire: switch S1 is closed, so electricity can reach the branches. Then check each branch. Lamp W's branch has an open switch (S2), so W is off. Lamps X and Y are in series on the same branch, and that branch is complete, so both light (they share the push, so they are dimmer). Lamp Z's branch has a closed switch (S3), so Z lights. The lit lamps are X, Y and Z.

misconceptions.0: Lamp W's branch has an open switch, so there is a gap and W stays off.
misconceptions.common: Thinking one open switch turns off every lamp. A switch on a branch only breaks that branch. The main switch S1 is closed, so the other branches still work, including the branch with two lamps.

questions.prompt: Look at the series circuit. Kumar takes out one lamp and joins the wires so that the loop is complete again. What happens to the two lamps that are left?
options: They stay exactly as bright as before
questions.solution: Before, the push from one cell was shared by three lamps. After Kumar takes one out, the same push is shared by only two lamps, so each lamp gets more and both become brighter. The loop is complete again, so they still light.

misconceptions.1: Fewer lamps in series means each lamp gets a bigger share of the push from the cell, so they get brighter, not dimmer.
misconceptions.2: Taking out a lamp changes the circuit. With fewer lamps sharing the cell, each lamp gets brighter.
misconceptions.3: Kumar joined the wires again, so the loop is complete and the lamps still light. They would only go out if a gap were left.

questions.prompt: Look at the series circuit. True or false: If you add a third identical lamp in series, each lamp becomes brighter.
questions.solution: False. In the diagram, two cells push electricity through two lamps. With a third lamp in the same loop, the same push is shared by three lamps, so each lamp becomes dimmer.

misconceptions.common: Thinking more lamps means more light from each one. In series the lamps share the push from the cells, so adding a lamp makes each lamp dimmer.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. How many cells are joined together in the battery? Give a whole number.

diagram.alt: A circuit diagram with a battery, a closed switch, two lamps and a buzzer joined in one loop.

questions.solution: Each cell is drawn as a long thin line next to a short thick line. Count these pairs of lines in the battery: there are 3, so the battery is made of 3 cells.

misconceptions.common: Counting all the components in the circuit, or the lines one by one. Count only the pairs of lines (one long, one short): each pair is one cell.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. Which component is the buzzer?

diagram.alt: A circuit diagram with a battery and three other components, labelled P, Q and R, joined in one loop.

options: There is no buzzer in this circuit
questions.solution: Name each labelled symbol. P is a circle with the letter M inside: a motor. R is a short line lying flat across a gap: a closed switch. Q is the buzzer symbol, so Q is the buzzer.

misconceptions.0: P is a circle with the letter M inside. That is the symbol for a motor.
misconceptions.2: R is a short line lying flat across a gap. That is a closed switch.
misconceptions.3: There is a buzzer: component Q. Its symbol is different from the lamp and motor circles.

questions.prompt: Ahmad builds the circuit shown, but neither lamp lights. He thinks lamp X is broken. Look at the diagram. What is the most likely reason the lamps are off?
options: The switch is open, so there is a gap in the loop
The battery has too many cells for two lamps
Lamp Y is too far away from the battery
Lamp X uses up all the electricity before it reaches lamp Y
questions.solution: Check the diagram for gaps before blaming a lamp. The switch symbol has its short line lifted, so the switch is open and the loop has a gap. No electricity can flow, so both lamps are off. Closing the switch should make both lamps light.

misconceptions.1: Two cells are fine for two lamps; they would light them quite brightly. Look for a gap in the loop instead.
misconceptions.2: The length of the wire to a lamp does not stop it lighting. Look at the switch symbol: it is open.
misconceptions.3: Electricity is not used up by the first lamp. Lamp X is off too, which tells you there is a gap somewhere in the loop.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. Lamps A and C light, but lamp B does not. All the wires are joined properly. What is the most likely fault?
options: Lamps A and C take all the electricity, so none is left for lamp B
questions.solution: Test each idea against what you see. If the cell were flat, no lamp would light. The switch is in the main wire, so if it were open, all three lamps would be off. But A and C are lit, so the cell and the switch are fine. Only lamp B's own branch is not working, so the most likely fault is that lamp B is broken.

misconceptions.1: If the cell were flat, none of the lamps would light. A and C are lit, so the cell is working.
misconceptions.2: The switch is in the main wire before the circuit splits. If it were open, all three lamps would be off.
misconceptions.3: In a parallel circuit each branch gets the full push of the cell. Lamps do not use up the electricity meant for the other branches.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. Which object, clipped across gap X, will make the lamp light?
questions.solution: The gap breaks the loop, so the lamp is off. To make the lamp light, the object across the gap must be an electrical conductor. Steel is a metal, so the steel key conducts and completes the loop.

misconceptions.0: Rubber is an electrical insulator, so the loop stays broken and the lamp stays off.
misconceptions.1: Plastic is an electrical insulator, so the loop stays broken and the lamp stays off.
misconceptions.2: Dry wood is an electrical insulator, so the loop stays broken and the lamp stays off.

questions.prompt: Look at circuits A to E. All the parts work. Select ALL the circuits in which the buzzer will sound.
questions.solution: The buzzer sounds only if there is a complete path from the cell, through the buzzer and back. Circuit A is a complete loop with a closed switch. In circuit C the buzzer has its own complete branch. In B the single loop has an open switch; in D the open switch is on the buzzer's own branch; in E the open switch is in the main wire, so no branch works. So the buzzer sounds in A and C.

misconceptions.1: Circuit B is a single loop with an open switch, so there is a gap and the buzzer is silent.
misconceptions.3: In circuit D the open switch is on the buzzer's own branch, so the buzzer's path is broken. (The lamp on the other branch still lights.)
misconceptions.4: In circuit E the open switch is in the main wire before the circuit splits, so neither branch works.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. How many lamps are lit (even if some glow dimly)? Give a whole number.
questions.solution: The switch in the main wire is closed, so check each branch. The branch with two lamps is complete, so both of its lamps light: 2. The branch with an open switch has a gap, so its lamp is off: 0. The branch with a lamp and a buzzer is complete, so its lamp lights: 1. Total: 2 + 0 + 1 = 3 lamps.

misconceptions.common: Answering 4 by missing the open switch, or 2 by thinking the buzzer stops the lamp next to it. A buzzer is a working component: electricity flows through it, so the lamp on that branch lights.

questions.prompt: Look at the circuit diagram. All the lamps are identical. True or false: Lamp A is brighter than lamp B.
questions.solution: True. Lamp A is alone on its branch, so it gets the full push of the cell. Lamps B and C are in series on the other branch, so they share the push and each is dimmer. So lamp A is brighter than lamp B.

misconceptions.common: Thinking every lamp in a parallel circuit is equally bright. That is only true when each branch has one lamp. Two lamps in series on one branch share the push, so they are dimmer.

questions.prompt: Look at circuits A to D. Which one is a parallel circuit?

optionDiagrams.alt: Circuit A: a cell and two lamps, joined one after another in a single loop.
Circuit B: a cell, a closed switch and two lamps, joined one after another in a single loop.
Circuit C: a cell, with the wire splitting into two branches that each have one lamp.
Circuit D: a battery, a lamp and a buzzer, joined one after another in a single loop.

questions.solution: In a parallel circuit the wire splits into branches, and each branch is a separate path back to the cell. Circuit C splits into two branches with one lamp each, so it is a parallel circuit. Circuits A, B and D each have everything in one single loop, so they are series circuits.

misconceptions.0: Circuit A has its two lamps one after another in a single loop. That is a series circuit.
misconceptions.1: Circuit B has a switch, but everything is still in one single loop, so it is a series circuit.
misconceptions.3: Circuit D has a lamp and a buzzer in one loop with no branches, so it is a series circuit.
